knowledge_statements.title: Equality-Form Farkas Alternative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical exclusive alternative for a linear equality system with nonnegative unknowns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For 
\(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and 
\(b\in\mathbb R^m\), exactly one of the following systems has a solution:
\[
\text{(i) }Ax=b,\quad x\ge0;
\]
\[
\text{(ii) }A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\quad b^{\mathsf T}y<0.
\]
Thus either 
\(b\) is a nonnegative linear combination of the columns of 
\(A\), or a linear functional 
\(y\) is nonnegative on every column of 
\(A\) but strictly negative on 
\(b\). The second system is a finite certificate that the first system is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Either a nonnegative vector solves the equality system, or a separating multiplier certifies infeasibility, but never both.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of \(\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and \(\{y:A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y<0\}\) is nonempty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegative State-Price Characterization of No Arbitrage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-state asset-market characterization using the extract's nonnegative state-price condition; no normalization or strict-positivity assumption is added.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For assets \(i=1,\ldots,n\) with prices \(p_i\) and state returns \(r_{si}\), the absence-of-arbitrage condition holds if and only if there exists \(q=(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb{R}^m_+\) such that \(p_i=\sum_{s=1}^m q_sr_{si}\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absence of arbitrage is equivalent to the existence of a nonnegative state-price vector that prices every asset as the state-price-weighted sum of its state returns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{No arbitrage}\iff\exists q\in\mathbb{R}^m_+\ \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\ p_i=\sum_{s=1}^m q_sr_{si}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness Boundary for Strict Conic Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the strict conic alternative when finite generation or closedness is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Strict separation in the conic-hull Farkas alternative relies on closedness, which holds for every finitely generated cone. Without closedness the dichotomy can fail. Let
\[
C=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:v>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},\qquad b=(1,0).
\]
Then \(C\) is a convex cone and \(b\in\overline C\setminus C\). Every \(y\) satisfying \(y^{\mathsf T}c\ge0\) for all \(c\in C\) has \(y_1=0\) and \(y_2\ge0\), and therefore \(y^{\mathsf T}b=0\). Hence \(b\notin C\), but no functional is nonnegative on \(C\) and strictly negative at \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonclosed cone, an excluded boundary point may admit no strict separating Farkas witness.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is allowed to be a convex cone that is not finitely generated or closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cone nonmembership and strict separation need not be exhaustive without closedness.

notation.meaning: the nonclosed convex cone consisting of the open upper half-plane and the origin

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), the system \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0,\ y\ge0,\ y\ne0\) is feasible if and only if \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0,\ y\ge0,\ \mathbf1^{\mathsf T}y=1\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero nonnegative Gordan multiplier can be normalized to have component sum one.

children.title: Tucker Alternative
children.top_down_role: The homogeneous alternative associated with complementary support and strict-complementarity theory.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementary Witnesses Need Not Be Unique
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness of witnesses realizing a Tucker-type support partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Whenever a nonzero complementary witness pair \((x,s)\) exists with \(Ax=0\), \(x\ge0\), \(s=A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\), and \(x+s>0\), its realizing vectors need not be unique: positive rescaling already gives distinct witnesses, and higher-dimensional feasible faces may contain nonproportional witnesses with the same positive supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complementary support partition does not make its realizing vectors unique.
assumptions_latex: A nonzero complementary witness pair exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{support completion}\not\Rightarrow\text{unique realizing witnesses}.

notation.meaning: nonnegative vector in the transposed range

knowledge_statements.title: Complementary Witnesses Need Not Be Unique

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a complementary pair whose combined support is every coordinate.

notation.meaning: nonnegative vector in the transposed range

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementary-support form of Tucker's homogeneous theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), there exist \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that, with \(s=A^{\mathsf T}y\), \[Ax=0,\qquad x\geq0,\qquad s\geq0,\qquad x+s>0.\] Consequently \(x^{\mathsf T}s=x^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}y=0\); hence \(x_i s_i=0\) for every coordinate \(i\), while \(x_i+s_i>0\) ensures that exactly one of \(x_i\) and \(s_i\) is positive. Thus their positive supports form a partition of the coordinate set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative null vector and a nonnegative transposed-range vector can be chosen complementary, with their positive supports covering every coordinate.
knowledge_statements.title: Tucker Alternative

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complementary-support statement is consistent with a Tucker-type homogeneous theorem and has compatible dimensions, but the exact variant and attribution are unsupported. The statement also contains derivational proof text that should be removed from a sourced replacement.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed maximal-support form of Tucker's homogeneous theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(K=\{x:Ax=0,\ x\ge0\}\) and \(R=\{s:s=A^{\mathsf T}y\text{ for some }y,\ s\ge0\}\). Let \(P=\{i:\exists x\in K,\ x_i>0\}\) and \(Q=\{i:\exists s\in R,\ s_i>0\}\). The proposed Tucker support-completion statement asserts \(P\dot\cup Q=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and the existence of witnesses whose positive supports are exactly \(P\) and \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proposed Tucker formulation partitions coordinates between maximal supports of the nonnegative null cone and nonnegative transposed range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\dot\cup Q=\{1,\ldots,n\}.

notation.meaning: nonnegative part of the transposed range

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Tucker Support Partition

LP strict complementarity is excluded, and Gordan and Stiemke remain sibling scopes; the topic is therefore deferred.

children.title: Strict-Relation Alternatives

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform-Margin Form of Finite Strict Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent margin representation of a finite strict inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(m>0\), \[\exists x:\ Ax<b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists(x,\varepsilon):\ Ax\le b-\varepsilon\mathbf1,\ \varepsilon>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite strict system is feasible exactly when all rows admit one common positive slack margin.
assumptions_latex: The strict system has finitely many nonzero-count rows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict feasibility is equivalent to existence of a uniform positive margin.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Margin Form of Finite Strict Feasibility

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict feasibility holds exactly when every nonzero nonnegative left-null multiplier has positive right-hand-side pairing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Purely strict affine inequality specialization of transposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The strict system \(Ax<b\) has a solution \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) if and only if every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \(y\geq0\), \(y\neq0\), and \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) also satisfies \(b^{\mathsf T}y>0\). Equivalently, exactly one of the following holds: \[Ax<b\text{ for some }x,\] or \[y\geq0,\quad y\neq0,\quad A^{\mathsf T}y=0,\quad b^{\mathsf T}y\leq0\text{ for some }y.\] All order relations are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict affine inequalities are feasible exactly when every nonzero nonnegative dependence among their normals pairs positively with the bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Relation Alternatives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strict-system criterion and its certificate side are mathematically plausible, but no source confirms this exact Motzkin specialization. An authoritative theorem locator is needed, and theorem is the more exact content kind for this terminal.

The strict scalar inequality in the certificate is essential: a zero pairing does not contradict a feasible non-strict system. This is the non-strict-relation specialization of the mixed transposition theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A non-strict inequality system is infeasible exactly when a nonnegative dependence among its normals yields a strictly negative bound combination.

children.title: Mixed-Relation Alternatives
children.top_down_role: Alternative systems combining open and closed linear relations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common-Margin Representation of a Finite Mixed System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent margin representation of finite mixed strict and non-strict inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(C\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^p\), and \(d\in\mathbb R^q\), with \(q>0\), \[\exists x:\ Ax\le b,\ Cx<d\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists(x,\varepsilon):\ Ax\le b,\ Cx\le d-\varepsilon\mathbf1,\ \varepsilon>0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite mixed system is feasible exactly when all strict rows admit a common positive margin while the weak rows remain unchanged.
assumptions_latex: The strict block is nonempty and finite, and inequalities are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Mixed strict feasibility is equivalent to feasibility with a common positive margin on the strict block.

notation.meaning: Common positive margin for the strict rows.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Margin Representation of a Finite Mixed System

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one of the mixed system and the stated Motzkin certificate is feasible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite mixed strict and non-strict Motzkin alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \[Ax\leq b,\qquad Cx<d\quad\text{for some }x\in\mathbb{R}^n;\] or \[y\geq0,\quad z\geq0,\quad A^{\mathsf T}y+C^{\mathsf T}z=0,\quad \beta=b^{\mathsf T}y+d^{\mathsf T}z\leq0,\] where additionally \(z\neq0\) or \(\beta<0\). The disjunction in the last condition records the strict block: a nonzero strict-block multiplier permits a zero scalar pairing, whereas a certificate supported only on non-strict relations must give a strictly negative pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed strict and non-strict inequalities are infeasible exactly when nonnegative multipliers satisfy balance, nonpositive bounds, and the strictness side condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Relation Alternatives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated balance, bound, and strict-block side conditions match a standard form of Motzkin transposition, but the exact convention is source-sensitive and no citation is supplied. An authoritative locator must confirm the formula; the final content kind should be theorem.

children.title: Strictness Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural limits governing substitutions between strict and non-strict formulations.

assumptions_latex: Strict and non-strict inequalities are interpreted componentwise over \(\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The multiplier side condition cannot be removed or uniformly replaced by strict negativity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinction between strict and non-strict multiplier conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the strict system \[x<0,\qquad -x<0.\] It is infeasible, and \(y=(1,1)^{\mathsf T}\geq0\) satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and pairs with the zero right-hand side to give \(0\), not a negative number. Thus requiring strict negativity would miss a valid strict-system certificate. Conversely, the non-strict system \[x\leq0,\qquad -x\leq0\] is feasible at \(x=0\), although the same nonzero multiplier has zero pairing. Hence allowing zero pairing without requiring positive weight on a strict relation would falsely certify infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero multiplier pairing can certify an infeasible strict system but cannot certify an analogous non-strict system; the Motzkin side condition is indispensable.
knowledge_statements.title: Strictness Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Both examples are internally correct and sharply distinguish strict from non-strict certificate conditions, and failure_boundary fits the terminal. However, the nontrivial sharpness claim has no source record or inspectable locator.

children.title: Classical Specializations of Motzkin Transposition
children.top_down_role: The recovery of Farkas and homogeneous alternatives as structured special cases.

assumptions_latex: All matrices and vectors are finite-dimensional and all order relations are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deleting relation blocks or fixing their right-hand sides recovers the stated classical alternatives.

notation.meaning: multipliers of non-strict and strict blocks

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specialization map from Motzkin transposition to classical alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start with the mixed system \(Ax\leq b\), \(Cx<d\) and its Motzkin multipliers \((y,z)\). Setting the strict block empty gives the inequality-form Farkas alternative, because the remaining certificate must satisfy \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\). Setting the non-strict block empty gives the strict-relation alternative, where \(z\neq0\) permits \(d^{\mathsf T}z=0\). Choosing zero right-hand sides produces homogeneous alternatives: the strict block yields Gordan's nonzero nonnegative null multiplier, while transposition and exchange of primal and multiplier spaces yields the positive-null-vector form associated with Stiemke.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Farkas, Gordan, and Stiemke forms arise from Motzkin transposition by deleting blocks, setting bounds to zero, and transposing systems.
knowledge_statements.title: Classical Specializations of Motzkin Transposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The specialization map is plausible and representation is an appropriate content kind, but the transitions among Motzkin, Farkas, Gordan, and Stiemke forms depend on exact sign and naming conventions. No authoritative locator supports the complete map.

children.title: Slack Transformations
children.top_down_role: Passages between inequality and equality representations through slack objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Slack Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of one-sided inequalities into equalities with nonnegative slack variables, including the corresponding alternative certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\),
\[
\exists x\in\mathbb R^n:\ Ax\le b
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists (x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+^m:\ Ax+s=b.
\]
The correspondence sends a feasible \(x\) to \((x,b-Ax)\) and projects a feasible \((x,s)\) to \(x\). Applying the equality-system alternative to \(Ax+s=b\), with \(x\) free and \(s\ge0\), yields the infeasibility certificate
\[
y\ge0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y=0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y<0,
\]
which is exactly the alternative certificate for \(Ax\le b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a nonnegative slack converts each inequality into an equality without changing feasibility, and the resulting equality-system multiplier conditions reproduce the original inequality-system infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\le b\) and \(Ax+s=b,\ s\ge0\) are feasibility-equivalent and have the displayed common alternative certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Slack Lifting Is a Graph Embedding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness of the auxiliary slack in the inequality-to-equality transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\},\qquad
\widetilde F=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R_+^m:Ax+s=b\},
\]
the map
\[
x\longmapsto (x,b-Ax)
\]
is a bijection from \(F\) onto \(\widetilde F\), with inverse \((x,s)\mapsto x\). Hence the slack vector is uniquely determined by the original feasible point; unlike free-variable splitting, slack introduction creates no representation fibers over \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The slack formulation is the graph of the residual map, so each original feasible point has exactly one lifted slack representation.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and inequalities are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual map \(x\mapsto b-Ax\) gives a bijection between the original inequality feasible set and its slack-lifted equality representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Slack Lifting Is a Graph Embedding

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m,n\in\mathbb N\), let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a Cartesian product of free, nonnegative, and nonpositive coordinate domains. Replace a free coordinate \(x_j\in\mathbb R\) by \(z_j^+-z_j^-\) with \(z_j^+,z_j^-\ge0\), a nonpositive coordinate by \(-z_j\) with \(z_j\ge0\), and a nonnegative coordinate by \(z_j\ge0\). These substitutions define a surjective linear map \(T:\mathbb R_+^q\to D\) for some \(q\in\mathbb N\), and
\[
\exists x\in D:\ Ax=b
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\mathbb R_+^q:\ ATz=b.
\]
For every \(y\in\mathbb R^m\), the condition \((AT)^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\) is equivalent to the coordinatewise sign-appropriate conditions on \(A^{\mathsf T}y\); the two columns used for a free coordinate force the corresponding component of \(A^{\mathsf T}y\) to equal zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit signed substitutions map a nonnegative transformed variable vector onto the original mixed-sign domain. They preserve feasibility, and their transformed multiplier inequalities reproduce the correct equality or one-sided condition for every original coordinate.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign Transformations

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3 Reduction to inequality system p. 19
source_witnesses.source_title: Interior Point Methods for Linear Optimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representational redundancy created by expressing an unrestricted coordinate as a difference of nonnegative coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the substitution \(x_j=z_j^+-z_j^-\) with \(z_j^+,z_j^-\ge0\), every \(\alpha\ge0\) satisfies
\[
(z_j^++\alpha)-(z_j^-+\alpha)=x_j.
\]
Thus the sign-substitution map is surjective but generally not injective. It preserves feasibility after projection, but uniqueness of lifted representations, boundedness of nonempty lifted fibers, and representation-sensitive geometric properties do not follow. A single-valued inverse requires an additional representative-selection convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting a free variable into positive and negative parts preserves feasibility but creates redundant, unbounded fibers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The free-variable splitting map is surjective and generally noninjective, so feasibility is preserved but lifted representations are nonunique.

notation.meaning: nonnegative positive and negative parts of a free coordinate
common nonnegative increment along a representation fiber

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(k\in\mathbb N\) and let \(S_0,S_1,\ldots,S_k\) be finite-dimensional linear systems. For every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), suppose
\[
S_{i-1}\text{ is feasible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S_i\text{ is feasible},
\]
where auxiliary variables may be existentially introduced, and suppose \(C_i\) maps every valid alternative certificate for \(S_i\) to a valid alternative certificate for \(S_{i-1}\). Then
\[
S_0\text{ is feasible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S_k\text{ is feasible},
\]
and every certificate for \(S_k\) pulls back to a certificate for \(S_0\) through
\[
C_1\circ C_2\circ\cdots\circ C_k.
\]
Different valid paths with the same endpoints may use different auxiliary variables or certificate normalizations while establishing the same endpoint feasibility alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite sequence of exact reformulations preserves feasibility between its endpoints. Certificate pullbacks compose in reverse through the sequence, although different paths may use different auxiliary variables or normalizations.
knowledge_statements.title: Transformation Equivalence Paths

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between chains of exact equivalences and paths containing a one-way relaxation or unsupported certificate step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Endpoint equivalence follows from a transformation path only when every step is an equivalence after its stated existential projection. A one-way feasibility implication is insufficient. For example, deleting the inconsistent row from \(0=1\) produces the feasible empty system: feasibility of \(0=1\) implies feasibility of the empty system, but the converse fails. Thus a path containing such a relaxation need not preserve endpoint infeasibility. Likewise, certificate transport across a step is justified only when a validity-preserving certificate map for that step is supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single one-way relaxation can break endpoint equivalence, and certificates cannot be transported through a step without a valid pullback map.
assumptions_latex: A proposed transformation path contains a step known only to preserve feasibility in one direction, or lacks a validity-preserving certificate pullback.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Such a path does not establish endpoint equivalence or certificate preservation.
knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Requirement for Equivalence Paths

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric identification of a conic Farkas infeasibility witness with a strict separating functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(K=A\mathbb R_+^n\). Since \(K\) is a finitely generated closed polyhedral cone, \[ b\notin K \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y\in\mathbb R^m:\ A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\quad b^{\mathsf T}y<0. \] The same vector \(y\) is therefore both a Farkas infeasibility multiplier and a linear functional nonnegative on \(K\) that strictly separates \(b\) from \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finitely generated cone, a Farkas infeasibility multiplier is exactly a functional that is nonnegative on the cone and strictly negative at the excluded point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\notin K\iff\exists y\in\mathbb R^m:\ A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y<0.\)

children.title: Alternative-Duality Equivalence
children.top_down_role: The foundational relationship between linear alternatives and LP strong duality.

assumptions_latex: \(m,n\in\mathbb N\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
All programs and alternative systems are finite-dimensional and real.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The universal equality-form Farkas alternative and finite-dimensional LP strong duality are logically equivalent assertions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical equivalence, over finite-dimensional linear programs, between Farkas alternatives and strong LP duality.

source_refs.locator: 6.2 Primal-Dual Relationships p. 264

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Over finite-dimensional real data, the following universal assertions are equivalent. First, for every \(m,n\in\mathbb N\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), exactly one of
\[
\exists x\in\mathbb R_+^n:\ Ax=b
\]
and
\[
\exists y\in\mathbb R^m:\ A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\quad b^{\mathsf T}y<0
\]
holds. Second, for every such \(A,b\) and every \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), if either member of the primal-dual pair
\[
\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},
\qquad
\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}
\]
is feasible with a finite optimal value, then both programs attain optimal solutions and their optimal values are equal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite-dimensional real linear programs, the universal equality-form Farkas alternative is logically equivalent to strong primal-dual attainment and value equality whenever one side has a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Alternative-Duality Equivalence

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m,n\in\mathbb N\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and define
\[
p^*=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in\mathbb R_+^n,\ Ax=b\}.
\]
Every \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[
A^{\mathsf T}y\le c
\]
is a dual bound witness and certifies
\[
b^{\mathsf T}y\le c^{\mathsf T}x
\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R_+^n\text{ with }Ax=b.
\]
Consequently, \(b^{\mathsf T}y\le p^*\) whenever the primal feasible set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual-feasible multiplier certifies a lower bound on every feasible primal objective value and therefore on the primal infimum whenever the primal is feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Bound Witnesses

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m,n\in\mathbb N\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). For the primal-dual pair
\[
\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in\mathbb R_+^n,\ Ax=b\},
\qquad
\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:y\in\mathbb R^m,\ A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\},
\]
let \(x\in\mathbb R_+^n\) satisfy \(Ax=b\), let \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfy \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\), and let \(p^*\) denote the primal optimal value. Then
\[
b^{\mathsf T}y\le p^*\le c^{\mathsf T}x.
\]
The pair \((x,y)\) is an interval certificate whose certified width is
\[
g(x,y):=c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y
=(c-A^{\mathsf T}y)^{\mathsf T}x\ge0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-feasible point and a dual-feasible multiplier certify lower and upper bounds on the primal optimum. Their objective difference is the nonnegative width of the certified interval.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Bound Pairs

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Individual Suboptimality Bounds from a Primal-Dual Pair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-error consequences of an exact feasible primal-dual interval certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
\min\{c^{\mathsf T}z:Az=b,\ z\ge0\},\qquad
\max\{b^{\mathsf T}w:A^{\mathsf T}w\le c\},
\]
let \(x\) be primal feasible and \(y\) dual feasible. Let \(p^*\) denote their common finite optimal value and define \(g(x,y)=c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y\). Then
\[
0\le c^{\mathsf T}x-p^*\le g(x,y),\qquad
0\le p^*-b^{\mathsf T}y\le g(x,y).
\]
Consequently, if \(g(x,y)\le\varepsilon\), both feasible objective values are within \(\varepsilon\) of \(p^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The width of a feasible primal-dual bracket bounds the objective suboptimality of each endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le c^{\mathsf T}x-p^*\le g(x,y)\) and \(0\le p^*-b^{\mathsf T}y\le g(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Individual Suboptimality Bounds from a Primal-Dual Pair

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m,n\in\mathbb N\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). For the primal-dual pair
\[
\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in\mathbb R_+^n,\ Ax=b\},
\qquad
\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:y\in\mathbb R^m,\ A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\},
\]
a pair \((x,y)\in\mathbb R_+^n\times\mathbb R^m\) is a zero-gap certificate if
\[
Ax=b,
\quad A^{\mathsf T}y\le c,
\quad c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y.
\]
Every zero-gap certificate identifies \(x\) and \(y\) as optimal solutions of their respective programs and identifies their common objective value as the finite optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and equality of the two objective values form a zero-gap certificate of optimality for both points.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Gap Primal-Dual Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m,n\in\mathbb N\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). For the primal-dual pair
\[
\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in\mathbb R_+^n,\ Ax=b\},
\qquad
\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:y\in\mathbb R^m,\ A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\},
\]
define \(s=c-A^{\mathsf T}y\in\mathbb R^n\). A triple \((x,y,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\) is a complementarity certificate if
\[
Ax=b,
\quad x\ge0,
\quad A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,
\quad s\ge0,
\quad x_js_j=0\quad\text{for every }j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}.
\]
These conditions are equivalent to primal-dual feasibility with zero objective gap, and they certify that \(x\) and \(y\) are optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-feasible point, a dual-feasible multiplier, and its nonnegative dual slack form a complementarity certificate when every primal variable has zero product with its corresponding slack. This is equivalent to a zero-gap optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m,n\in\mathbb N\) with \(m\le n\), let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have row rank \(m\), and let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). Consider
\[
\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in\mathbb R_+^n,\ Ax=b\}.
\]
Let \(\mathcal B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) have cardinality \(m\), let \(\mathcal N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal B\), let \(B=A_{\mathcal B}\) be nonsingular, and let \(N=A_{\mathcal N}\). Define
\[
x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b,
\quad x_{\mathcal N}=0,
\quad y=B^{-\mathsf T}c_{\mathcal B},
\quad r_{\mathcal N}=c_{\mathcal N}-N^{\mathsf T}y.
\]
If
\[
x_{\mathcal B}\ge0
\quad\text{and}\quad
r_{\mathcal N}\ge0,
\]
then \((\mathcal B,x,y,r_{\mathcal N})\) is a basis optimality certificate for the associated basic feasible solution. The certificate remains valid when the basic feasible solution is degenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-row-rank standard-form minimization problem, a nonsingular basis certifies optimality when its basic solution and all nonbasic reduced costs are nonnegative. Degeneracy does not invalidate the certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Optimality Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate Optimal Point with a Noncertifying Basis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that optimality of a degenerate basic feasible point does not make every representing feasible basis dual feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
\min\{-x_2:x_1+x_2=0,\ x_1,x_2\ge0\}.
\]
Its unique feasible and hence optimal point is \(x=(0,0)\). The basis \(\mathcal B=\{1\}\) is nonsingular and primal feasible, with \(B=[1]\), \(c_{\mathcal B}=0\), and basis multiplier \(y=0\). Its nonbasic reduced cost is
\[
r_2=c_2-A_2^{\mathsf T}y=-1<0.
\]
Thus this basis does not furnish a basis optimality certificate even though its associated degenerate basic feasible point is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate optimal point may be represented by a primal-feasible basis having a negative reduced cost, so the point's optimality does not make every representing basis an optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x=(0,0)\text{ is optimal, but }r_2=-1<0\text{ for the feasible basis }\mathcal B=\{1\}.

\[
\widetilde y=\frac{y}{-b^{\mathsf T}y}

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Improving Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-form primal minimization and its inequality-form dual maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the primal-dual pair 
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\},\qquad \max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}.\]
Given a dual-feasible point \(y_0\), a vector \(d\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}d\le 0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}d>0\) is a dual improving ray. For every \(t\ge0\), the point \(y_0+td\) is dual feasible and its objective value is \(b^{\mathsf T}y_0+t b^{\mathsf T}d\), which tends to \(+\infty\). Thus \((y_0,d)\) certifies dual unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible dual point plus a direction preserving dual feasibility and strictly increasing the objective certifies that the dual is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}=+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete equality-form LP pair showing that both sides may be infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the scalar equality-form pair
\[\min\{-x:0x=1,\ x\ge0\},\qquad \max\{y:0y\le-1\},\]
the primal constraint \(0x=1\) is inconsistent, while the dual constraint \(0\le-1\) is inconsistent. Hence both members of a legitimate primal-dual LP pair can be infeasible simultaneously; neither side then has an improving feasible ray because neither side has a feasible base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pair with zero constraint matrix, right-hand side one, and cost minus one makes both primal and dual infeasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the pair
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\qquad \max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\},\]
primal infeasibility alone does not imply dual unboundedness, and dual infeasibility alone does not imply primal unboundedness. The instance \(A=0\), \(b=1\), and \(c=-1\) has both sides infeasible, so it supplies both counterimplications. Opposite-side unboundedness requires feasibility of that side in addition to an improving recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One side being infeasible does not make the other unbounded; the other side may also be infeasible.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual use the displayed equality-form convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ infeasible}\not\Rightarrow D\text{ unbounded}\) and \(D\text{ infeasible}\not\Rightarrow P\text{ unbounded}\).

source_refs.locator: 6. Duality of Linear Programming p. 81

source_witnesses.locator: 6. Duality of Linear Programming p. 81

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility Completes the Converse Status Classification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp finite-dimensional LP refinement of the invalid bare-infeasibility converses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the finite-dimensional pair \[P=\inf\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\qquad D=\sup\{b^\top y:A^\top y\le c\},\] the sharpened implications are \[F_P=\varnothing\ \land\ F_D\ne\varnothing\ \Longrightarrow\ \sup D=+\infty,\] and \[F_D=\varnothing\ \land\ F_P\ne\varnothing\ \Longrightarrow\ \inf P=-\infty.\] Thus feasibility of the opposite side is the missing hypothesis in each invalid converse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-sided infeasibility forces opposite-side unboundedness when the opposite side is also known to be feasible.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ and }D\text{ use the displayed finite-dimensional LP convention}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (F_P=\varnothing,F_D\ne\varnothing)\Rightarrow\sup D=+\infty,\quad(F_D=\varnothing,F_P\ne\varnothing)\Rightarrow\inf P=-\infty
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Completes the Converse Status Classification

children.title: Problem Status Versus Returned Certificate
children.top_down_role: The distinction between exact mathematical status and the witness exposed by a formulation or solver.

knowledge_statements.title: Problem Status Versus Returned Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates an exact LP status from the particular witness reported by an algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be an exact LP status for data \((A,b,c)\), and let \(C_S(w;A,b,c)\) be a sound, status-specific certificate predicate. A returned witness \(w\) establishes \(S\) only when the exact check \(C_S(w;A,b,c)\) succeeds. A solver label alone is not a certificate, and failure to return a witness does not imply that \(S\) is false.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact LP status is established by a returned witness only when that witness passes a sound, status-specific certificate check; a solver label or absence of a witness is not conclusive by itself.
assumptions_latex: \((A,b,c)\) and the entries of \(w\) have an exact interpretation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_S(w;A,b,c)\Rightarrow S(A,b,c)\).

notation.meaning: sound certificate predicate for status S

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validation condition for certificates produced after presolve, scaling, reformulation, or embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) transform an original LP \(L\) into a working formulation \(\widehat L\), and let \(\widehat w\) satisfy a certificate predicate for \(\widehat L\). The witness establishes the corresponding status of \(L\) only if a verified recovery map produces \(w=R(\widehat w)\) and the original-data predicate \(C_S(w;A,b,c)\) succeeds. Validation solely against \(\widehat L\) is not by itself an original-problem certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate from a transformed model certifies the original LP only after sound recovery and validation against the original data.
assumptions_latex: \widehat w\text{ is a witness for }\widehat L
C_S\text{ is sound for status }S\text{ of the original LP}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_S(R(\widehat w);A,b,c)\Rightarrow S(L)
knowledge_statements.title: Original-Form Certificate Validation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tolerance Checks Do Not Establish Exact Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between numerical diagnostic acceptance and an exact mathematical LP certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a floating-point witness \(\widetilde w\) satisfies residual tests only to declared positive tolerances, such as \(\|r_P(\widetilde w)\|\le\varepsilon_P\) and \(\|r_D(\widetilde w)\|\le\varepsilon_D\), or satisfies a strict certificate margin only after tolerance adjustment. These tests establish an approximate acceptance condition but do not alone imply the corresponding exact equalities, inequalities, or strict margins. Exact status follows only from exact verification or rigorous error bounds implying the exact certificate predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Passing floating-point tolerance tests is diagnostic evidence, not an exact LP status certificate unless rigorous bounds imply the exact predicate.
assumptions_latex: \widetilde w\text{ is evaluated using non-rigorous floating-point residual tests}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{tolerance acceptance}\not\Rightarrow C_S(\widetilde w;A,b,c)\quad\text{without exact verification or rigorous error bounds}
knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance Checks Do Not Establish Exact Status

children.title: Polyhedral Strong-Infeasibility Boundary
children.top_down_role: The LP boundary supported by closed polyhedral geometry and ordinary separating certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Strong-Infeasibility Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polyhedral systems exclude weak infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P,Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty polyhedra. If \(P\cap Q=\varnothing\), then their Euclidean distance is strictly positive and is attained:
\[\operatorname{dist}(P,Q)=\min\{\|p-q\|_2:p\in P,\ q\in Q\}>0.\]
Consequently, infeasibility of a finite-dimensional linear system admits strict affine separation and an ordinary finite Farkas-type certificate. The zero-distance, unattained separation phenomenon called weak infeasibility therefore does not occur between polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjoint nonempty polyhedra have positive attained distance, so infeasible LP systems admit strict separating certificates rather than weak infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) are nonempty polyhedra in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(P,Q)>0\), with the minimum attained.

notation.meaning: infimum Euclidean distance between the two sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological property of polyhedra in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every polyhedron $P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every polyhedron in finite-dimensional Euclidean space is a closed set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is closed}

children.title: Weak Infeasibility Outside Linear Programming
children.top_down_role: A boundary marker for nonpolyhedral conic systems requiring broader infeasibility theory.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Exact Duals and Short Certificates of Infeasibility and Weak Infeasibility in Conic Linear Programming

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-based boundary between weak and strong infeasibility for finite-dimensional conic systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^N\) be a closed convex cone and \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^N\) a nonempty affine subspace. The system is strongly infeasible when \(L\cap K=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(L,K)>0\), and weakly infeasible when \(L\cap K=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak infeasibility means that the affine space misses the cone but approaches it arbitrarily closely; strong infeasibility has positive separation distance.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^N\text{ is a closed convex cone}
L\subseteq\mathbb R^N\text{ is a nonempty affine subspace}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\cap K=\varnothing,\quad \operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0\text{ defines weak infeasibility, while }\operatorname{dist}(L,K)>0\text{ defines strong infeasibility}

notation.meaning: infimum of distances between points of the affine space and cone

knowledge_statements.title: Weak and Strong Conic Infeasibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary strict conic separation certifies strong, not weak, infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write \(L=x_0+V\) and let \(K^*=\{z:\langle z,k\rangle\ge0\ \forall k\in K\}\). If \(z\in K^*\cap V^\perp\) satisfies \(\langle z,x_0\rangle<0\), then \(\operatorname{dist}(L,K)>0\). Hence a weakly infeasible system admits no such strict separator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict dual separator proves positive-distance infeasibility and therefore cannot exist for a weakly infeasible system.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^N\text{ is a closed convex cone}
L=x_0+V\text{ is a nonempty affine subspace}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists z\in K^*\cap V^\perp:\langle z,x_0\rangle<0\bigr)\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}(L,K)>0

notation.meaning: orthogonal complement of the direction space of L

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Separation Failure at Weak Infeasibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonpolyhedral weakly infeasible affine conic system distinct from the deferred semidefinite example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R^3:u\ge\sqrt{v^2+w^2}\}\) and \(L=\{(t,1,t):t\in\mathbb R\}\). Then \(L\cap K=\varnothing\). Moreover, for \(t>0\), \((\sqrt{1+t^2},1,t)\in K\) and its distance from \((t,1,t)\in L\) is \(\sqrt{1+t^2}-t\to0\). Consequently \(\operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine line misses the Lorentz cone while approaching it arbitrarily closely, giving weak infeasibility outside LP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\cap K=\varnothing,\qquad \operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0.

notation.meaning: affine line of candidate conic points

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order-Cone Weak Infeasibility Example
Weak Infeasibility Outside Linear Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A semidefinite feasibility example marking the nonpolyhedral boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the semidefinite feasibility system
\[X(t)=\begin{pmatrix}t&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\succeq0,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.\]
It is infeasible because every \(X(t)\) has determinant \(-1\), whereas a positive-semidefinite matrix has nonnegative determinant. Nevertheless, the negative eigenvalue of \(X(t)\) tends to \(0\) as \(t\to+\infty\), so the distance from the affine family \(\{X(t):t\in\mathbb R\}\) to the positive-semidefinite cone is zero. This is weak infeasibility, a phenomenon absent for polyhedral LP systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine family of two-by-two matrices can miss the positive-semidefinite cone while having zero distance from it.
assumptions_latex: Distance is measured using the Frobenius norm on symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{X(t):t\in\mathbb R\}\cap\mathbb S_+^2=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(\{X(t)\},\mathbb S_+^2)=0\).

notation.meaning: cone of real two-by-two positive-semidefinite matrices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The semidefinite example is mathematically plausible and appropriately classified, but it has no citation. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required for this nonpolyhedral weak-infeasibility claim.

children.title: Certificate Scale Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Equivalence classes of certificate representatives under admissible rescaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Scale Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive rescaling of homogeneous LP status witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a certificate is defined by homogeneous linear constraints \(Mw=0\), \(Nw\ge0\), together with a strict homogeneous condition \(q^{\mathsf T}w>0\). If \(w\) is a certificate, then \(\alpha w\) is a certificate for every \(\alpha>0\). Conversely, any two representatives on the same positive ray encode the same certified status. A normalization may select one representative without changing validity, provided its normalizing functional is positive on the nonzero certificate cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive multiples of a homogeneous certificate are equivalent, and normalization merely chooses one representative of the same ray.
assumptions_latex: The certificate predicates are homogeneous in \(w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w\sim\alpha w\) and \(\operatorname{valid}(w)\iff\operatorname{valid}(\alpha w)\).

source_refs.locator: 4.10. General linear programming duality* p. 183

source_witnesses.locator: 4.10. General linear programming duality* p. 183

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-ray equivalence generally does not extend to negative scale factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a homogeneous certificate containing \(Nw\geq0\) and \(q^{\mathsf T}w>0\), multiplication by \(\alpha<0\) reverses the inequality and strict-margin signs. Unless the certificate system has an additional sign symmetry, \(w\) and \(\alpha w\) therefore need not have the same validity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative rescaling generally reverses sign-sensitive certificate predicates, so homogeneous certificate equivalence is positive-ray rather than line equivalence.
assumptions_latex: The certificate contains a sign-sensitive inequality or positive strict margin.
No additional sign symmetry identifies a witness with its negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In general, \(\operatorname{valid}(w)\not\Rightarrow\operatorname{valid}(\alpha w)\) for \(\alpha<0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Negative Rescaling Boundary

children.title: Certificate Normalization Conventions
children.top_down_role: Conventions selecting comparable representatives from scale-equivalent certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Normalization Conventions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard representatives for nonzero homogeneous certificate rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^k\) be a cone of valid homogeneous certificates and let \(w\in K\setminus\{0\}\). A scale-fixed representative may be chosen as
\[\widehat w=\frac{w}{\|w\|_1},\]
so that \(\|\widehat w\|_1=1\). If a linear functional \(q\) satisfies \(q^{\mathsf T}w>0\), one may instead use \(\widehat w=w/(q^{\mathsf T}w)\), giving \(q^{\mathsf T}\widehat w=1\). Either convention preserves all homogeneous certificate constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero homogeneous certificate can be normalized to unit one-norm or to make a positive certificate functional equal one.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is closed under multiplication by positive scalars.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat w\in K\) and either \(\|\widehat w\|_1=1\) or \(q^{\mathsf T}\widehat w=1\).

children.title: Nontrivial Witness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural boundary excluding zero or otherwise vacuous certificate representatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Nontrivial Witness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Excludes the zero vector from homogeneous certificate systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a homogeneous certificate system \(Mw=0\) and \(Nw\ge0\), validity requires \(w\ne0\). Nontriviality may instead be enforced by a strict predicate such as \(q^{\mathsf T}w>0\) when that predicate is required of every intended witness, or by a normalization such as \(\|w\|_1=1\). Without a zero-excluding condition, \(w=0\) satisfies every homogeneous equality and non-strict inequality but is not a separating, infeasibility, or improving-ray witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous witness must be nonzero, enforced directly or by a strict or normalized condition that excludes the zero vector.
assumptions_latex: All unnormalized certificate equalities and non-strict inequalities are homogeneous in \(w\).
Any substituted strict or normalized predicate excludes \(w=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{valid}(w)\Rightarrow w\ne0\).

notation.meaning: functional used in a strict zero-excluding predicate

children.title: Rational Certificate Encoding
children.top_down_role: Finite exact representations for rational LP certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Rational Certificate Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite encoding of witnesses for rational LP data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A,b,c\) are rational, a rational LP certificate \(w\in\mathbb Q^k\) can be stored exactly as signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Its defining rational linear equalities, inequalities, dot products, and objective comparisons can then be checked by exact arithmetic. For a homogeneous certificate, such as a Farkas vector or improving direction, clearing denominators produces a nonzero integer representative with the same validity. This scaling assertion does not apply to nonhomogeneous feasible-point equations with fixed right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational LP certificates have finite exact binary encodings and can be checked exactly; homogeneous certificates may additionally be scaled to integer representatives.
assumptions_latex: All entries of \(A,b,c\) and \(w\) are rational.
Certificate predicates are rational linear equalities, inequalities, dot products, or objective comparisons.
Denominator clearing is asserted only for predicates homogeneous in \(w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w\in\mathbb Q^k\) has a finite exact binary encoding, and homogeneous \(w\) has a positively scaled integer representative.

children.title: Short-Certificate Principle
children.top_down_role: The polynomially bounded witness perspective underlying efficient LP status verification.

knowledge_statements.title: Short-Certificate Principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial bit-length witnesses for exact rational LP statuses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a rational LP have total binary input length \(L\). Whenever it has a finite optimum, an infeasibility certificate, or an unboundedness certificate, it has a corresponding rational primal-dual basic solution, Farkas vector, or improving direction whose binary encoding length is bounded by a polynomial in \(L\). The defining linear equalities, inequalities, and objective relations can therefore be checked in time polynomial in \(L\) and the certificate length using exact integer or rational arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every standard status of a rational LP has a polynomial-size rational witness verifiable in polynomial time by exact arithmetic.
assumptions_latex: The LP data are rational and encoded in binary with total length \(L\).
Arithmetic complexity includes the bit lengths of intermediate integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{size}(w)\le\operatorname{poly}(L)\) and \(\operatorname{verify}(w)\) runs in \(\operatorname{poly}(L)\) bit operations.

notation.meaning: a polynomial bound in the input length

children.title: Exact-Numerical Validation Boundary
children.top_down_role: The boundary between exact certificate checking and tolerance-based numerical validation.

children.title: Exact Certificate Validation
children.top_down_role: Certificate checking under exact arithmetic and exact model data.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Certificate Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rational validation of optimality certificates for a standard-form primal-dual LP pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational data, consider the primal LP \\(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\\) and its dual \\(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\\). A rational tuple \\(x,y,s\\) is an exactly valid optimality certificate precisely when exact arithmetic verifies \\(Ax=b\\), \\(x\ge0\\), \\(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\\), \\(s\ge0\\), and \\(c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\\). Equivalently, after feasibility is established, the last equality may be replaced by \\(x^{\mathsf T}s=0\\). These identities certify that \\(x\\) and \\(y\\) are respectively primal and dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact rational feasibility and zero duality gap certify primal and dual optimality without tolerances or rounding decisions.
assumptions_latex: \\(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n},\ b\in\mathbb Q^m,\ c\in\mathbb Q^n\\)
All displayed equalities and inequalities are evaluated in exact rational arithmetic.

notation.meaning: dual optimal solution set in multiplier-slack coordinates

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact validation of a feasible point and improving recession ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), rational vectors \(x^0,d\) satisfying \(Ax^0=b\), \(x^0\ge0\), \(Ad=0\), \(d\ge0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\), all checked exactly, certify that the primal objective is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exactly feasible base point and strictly improving nonnegative null-space ray validate primal unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: All displayed predicates are checked in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}=-\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Primal-Unboundedness Validation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact validation of a Farkas witness for standard-form primal infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational \(A,b\), a rational vector \(y\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\), verified in exact arithmetic, certifies that \(\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact Farkas multiplier with nonnegative transpose product and negative right-hand-side pairing validates primal infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: All products, comparisons, and signs are checked exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y<0\Longrightarrow\nexists x\ge0:\ Ax=b.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Primal-Infeasibility Validation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial Bit Complexity of Exact Certificate Checking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verification cost for explicitly supplied rational LP witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the total binary encoding length of rational LP data and an explicitly supplied rational optimality, infeasibility, or unboundedness witness. Exact evaluation of its matrix-vector identities, sign conditions, and strict inequalities uses a number of bit operations polynomial in \(S\). This is a verification guarantee, not a witness-generation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit rational LP certificates can be checked in polynomial bit time independently of how they were produced.
assumptions_latex: All data and witness components are binary-encoded rationals.
The witness dimension is included in \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{verify}}=\operatorname{poly}(S).

notation.meaning: total encoding length of the instance and witness

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Bit Complexity of Exact Certificate Checking

children.title: Numerical Certificate Validation
children.top_down_role: Certificate checking under finite precision and tolerance-based acceptance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain guard for finite-precision residual and gap validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every supplied datum, candidate component, residual, scaling factor, norm, and objective-gap value used by a numerical certificate predicate must be finite. If any such quantity is NaN or \(\pm\infty\), the validator returns invalid or indeterminate rather than accepting the certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numerical validator must reject or mark indeterminate a certificate involving nonfinite inputs or test quantities.
assumptions_latex: Validation uses finite-precision values with distinguished NaN and infinite values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists q\text{ used by the predicate}:q\in\{\mathrm{NaN},+\infty,-\infty\}\bigr)\Longrightarrow\operatorname{status}\in\{\mathrm{invalid},\mathrm{indeterminate}\}.

notation.meaning: any scalar datum or computed validation quantity

knowledge_statements.title: Nonfinite-Value Rejection Condition
Numerical Certificate Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based validation of a floating-point candidate for a standard-form primal-dual LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \\(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\\) and its dual, let nonnegative tolerances \\(\tau_p,\tau_d,\tau_g\\) and fixed norms be specified. A floating-point tuple \\(\widehat x,\widehat y,\widehat s\\) passes numerical validation when \\(\|A\widehat x-b\|\le\tau_p\\), \\(\|(A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y+\widehat s)-c\|\le\tau_d\\), \\(\widehat x_i\ge-\tau_p\\), \\(\widehat s_i\ge-\tau_d\\) for every \\(i\\), and \\( |c^{\mathsf T}\widehat x-b^{\mathsf T}\widehat y|\le\tau_g\\). Passing certifies only conformance to these declared residual tests; it does not by itself establish exact feasibility or optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A floating-point certificate passes declared residual, sign, and gap thresholds, but this is not an exact optimality certificate.
assumptions_latex: The norms, scaling convention, and tolerances \\(\tau_p,\tau_d,\tau_g\ge0\\) are fixed before validation.
Residual computations have sufficient range to avoid unreported overflow or invalid values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(\operatorname{pass}_{\tau}(\widehat x,\widehat y,\widehat s)=\mathrm{true}\\)

notation.meaning: floating-point primal, dual-multiplier, and dual-slack candidates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a coherent declared residual test and correctly distinguishes numerical acceptance from exact optimality. However, the particular use of unscaled absolute residuals, shared feasibility/sign tolerances, and an absolute objective-gap tolerance is interface dependent, and no source is supplied to support this selected convention.

children.title: Tolerance Interpretation
children.top_down_role: Meaning and scope of feasibility, sign, and objective tolerances in certificate assessment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Absolute Residual Tests Are Not Representation Invariant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of rescaling an equivalent equation without rescaling its tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(ax=b\) and a candidate \(\hat x\) with residual \(r=a\hat x-b\ne0\). Replacing the equation by the equivalent equation \(\lambda ax=\lambda b\), where \(\lambda>0\), changes the absolute residual from \(|r|\) to \(\lambda|r|\). For a fixed \(\tau>0\), the original representation may satisfy \(|r|\le\tau\) while a sufficiently large \(\lambda\) makes \(\lambda|r|>\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed absolute residual tolerance can accept one scaling of an equation and reject an equivalent scaling.
assumptions_latex: The same positive absolute tolerance is used before and after row scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |r|\le\tau\not\Rightarrow\lambda|r|\le\tau.
knowledge_statements.title: Absolute Residual Tests Are Not Representation Invariant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension factors required when translating residual thresholds between common norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(r\in\mathbb R^q\), \(\|r\|_\infty\le\|r\|_2\le\sqrt q\,\|r\|_\infty\). Therefore \(\{r:\|r\|_2\le\tau\}\subseteq\{r:\|r\|_\infty\le\tau\}\subseteq\{r:\|r\|_2\le\sqrt q\,\tau\}\). The same numerical tolerance defines different residual neighborhoods under these norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tolerance values cannot be transferred unchanged between residual norms; dimension-dependent conversion factors are required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{r:\|r\|_2\le\tau\}\subseteq\{r:\|r\|_\infty\le\tau\}\subseteq\{r:\|r\|_2\le\sqrt q\,\tau\}.

Tolerance Interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Meaning of absolute and scaled tolerances in residual-based LP certificate checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tolerance is meaningful only together with its residual, norm, and scaling rule. For a residual \\(r(z)\\), an absolute test has the form \\(\|r(z)\|\le\tau_{\mathrm{abs}}\\), whereas a scaled test has the form \\(\|r(z)\|\le\tau_{\mathrm{abs}}+\tau_{\mathrm{rel}}\sigma(z)\\), where \\(\sigma(z)\ge0\\) is explicitly declared. Thus acceptance asserts membership in the corresponding residual neighborhood, not satisfaction of \\(r(z)=0\\). Comparisons of validators are mathematically well-defined only when their norms, scaling functions, data normalization, and absolute-versus-relative conventions agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tolerance defines a residual neighborhood only after its norm and scaling are fixed; acceptance never means exact equality.
assumptions_latex: \\(\sigma(z)\\) is a specified nonnegative scaling function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(\|r(z)\|\le\tau_{\mathrm{abs}}+\tau_{\mathrm{rel}}\sigma(z)\\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient rigorous conditions for promoting a computed primal-dual tuple to an exact certificate for intended exact data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) with dual equations \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), suppose sound directed enclosures are evaluated for the intended exact data. Exact optimality is certified if the primal- and dual-residual enclosures are the singleton \(\{0\}\), the lower endpoints of every enclosure for \(x_i\) and \(s_i\) are nonnegative, and the primal-dual gap enclosure is \(\{0\}\).

Validation Reliability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between residual-test acceptance and mathematically rigorous LP certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Residual-test acceptance is not a rigorous certificate of exact LP status unless rounding and data errors are converted into proved enclosures that imply the exact certificate relations. In particular, if a feasibility margin, reduced cost, or duality gap is comparable to the combined effects of tolerance, conditioning, input perturbation, and arithmetic error, the validator cannot reliably distinguish the exact relation from a nearby violated one. Reliability is recovered by exact arithmetic or by directed-error bounds proving primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and the required gap statement for the intended exact data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near the error scale, numerical residual tests cannot determine exact LP status; exact arithmetic or rigorous enclosures are required.
assumptions_latex: The intended LP data are exact or have explicitly bounded uncertainty.
Floating-point and residual errors are not silently treated as zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(\text{numerical pass}\not\Rightarrow\text{exact certificate validity}\\)

knowledge_statements.title: Strictly Complementary Optimal Pairs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form definition using primal variables and dual slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal-dual pair \\(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\\) and \\(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\\), an optimal tuple \\(x^*,y^*,s^*\\) is strictly complementary when, for every index \\(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\\), \\(x_i^*s_i^*=0\\) and \\(x_i^*+s_i^*>0\\). Equivalently, exactly one member of each complementary pair \\(x_i^*,s_i^*\\) is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly complementary optimal pair has exactly one positive member in every primal-variable and dual-slack coordinate pair.
assumptions_latex: \\(x^*\\) and \\((y^*,s^*)\\) are primal and dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(x_i^*s_i^*=0\ \text{and}\ x_i^*+s_i^*>0\quad\text{for all }i\\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior Characterization of Strictly Complementary Pairs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric characterization within the primal and dual-slack optimal faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_P\) be the primal optimal face of \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), and let \(F_S\) be the set of optimal dual slacks \(s=c-A^\top y\ge0\). An optimal tuple \((x,y,s)\) is strictly complementary if and only if \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(F_P)\) and \(s\in\operatorname{ri}(F_S)\). Equivalently, \(x\) is positive on every coordinate that can be positive at some primal optimum, and \(s\) is positive on every coordinate that can be positive at some optimal dual slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strictly complementary pairs are exactly the optimal pairs whose primal point and dual slack lie in the relative interiors of their respective optimal faces and realize their maximal supports.
assumptions_latex: The standard-form primal and dual attain a common finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x,y,s)\text{ is strictly complementary}\iff x\in\operatorname{ri}(F_P),\ s\in\operatorname{ri}(F_S).

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Complementarity Existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Goldman-Tucker existence theorem for finite-dimensional standard-form linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \\(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\\) and its dual \\(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\\). If both problems have optimal solutions with a common finite optimal value, then there exist optimal solutions \\(x^*\\) and \\((y^*,s^*)\\) such that \\(x_i^*+s_i^*>0\\) for every \\(i\\). Since complementary slackness gives \\(x_i^*s_i^*=0\\), this tuple is strictly complementary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Whenever the primal and dual attain the same finite optimum, at least one strictly complementary optimal pair exists.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual are finite-dimensional linear programs in the displayed standard form.
Both problems attain a common finite optimal value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(\exists(x^*,y^*,s^*)\ \forall i:\ x_i^*s_i^*=0\ \text{and}\ x_i^*+s_i^*>0\\)

children.top_down_role: The distinction between existence of a strictly complementary pair and behavior of arbitrary optimal pairs.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniversality Across Optimal Pairs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict complementarity exists but need not hold for every optimal pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \\(\min\{0:x_1+x_2=1,\ x\ge0\}\\). Its dual is \\(\max\{y:y+s_1=0,\ y+s_2=0,\ s\ge0\}\\), whose unique optimal multiplier-slack tuple is \\(y^*=0\\), \\(s^*=(0,0)\\). The optimal primal point \\(x=(1/2,1/2)\\) forms a strictly complementary pair with \\(s^*\\). However, the also-optimal point \\(x=(1,0)\\) does not, because \\(x_2+s_2^*=0\\). Thus existence of one strictly complementary pair does not make strict complementarity universal over all optimal pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate optimal face can contain both strictly complementary and non-strictly-complementary optimal points.
assumptions_latex: Optimal pairs are interpreted in standard-form primal-variable and dual-slack coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \\(\exists\text{ a strictly complementary optimal pair}\ \not\Rightarrow\ \forall\text{ optimal pairs, strict complementarity}\\)

children.title: Optimal-Face Dimension

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Face Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension formula for the primal optimal face in equality-form linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the primal program \(\max\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\) with a nonempty optimal face \(F_P\). Define \(J=\{j:\text{some }x\in F_P\text{ has }x_j>0\}\). Then a relative-interior point of \(F_P\) is positive exactly on \(J\), and
\[
\operatorname{aff}(F_P)=\{x:Ax=b,\ x_j=0\text{ for }j\notin J\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\dim F_P=|J|-\operatorname{rank}(A_J),
\]
where \(A_J\) is the submatrix formed by columns indexed by \(J\). In particular, the primal optimum is unique exactly when \(A_J\) has full column rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal face dimension equals the maximal optimal-support size minus the rank of the corresponding constraint columns; dimension zero is equivalent to a unique optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(F_P\neq\varnothing\) and the optimal value is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim F_P=|J|-\operatorname{rank}(A_J)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Constraint Patterns
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-constraint activity across a primal optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F_P\) be the nonempty optimal face of \(\max\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). For \(x\in F_P\), define its active nonnegativity pattern by \(I(x)=\{j:x_j=0\}\), and define \(I_F=\bigcap_{x\in F_P}I(x)\). Every optimal solution satisfies \(I_F\subseteq I(x)\), while
\[
x\in\operatorname{relint}(F_P)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad I(x)=I_F.
\]
Thus the constraints active throughout the face determine its affine hull, whereas additional active coordinates identify proper subfaces containing boundary optimal solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All optimal points share a core active set; relative-interior optima have exactly that set, while boundary optima activate additional nonnegativity constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{relint}(F_P)\iff I(x)=I_F\).

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Support Patterns
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support structure of solutions on the primal optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the nonempty optimal face \(F_P\), write \(\operatorname{supp}(x)=\{j:x_j>0\}\) and \(J=\bigcup_{x\in F_P}\operatorname{supp}(x)\). Every optimal support is contained in \(J\), and some \(\bar x\in\operatorname{relint}(F_P)\) satisfies \(\operatorname{supp}(\bar x)=J\). Moreover, if \(x^1,x^2\in F_P\) and \(0<\lambda<1\), then
\[
\operatorname{supp}(\lambda x^1+(1-\lambda)x^2)=\operatorname{supp}(x^1)\cup\operatorname{supp}(x^2).
\]
Hence the maximal optimal-support pattern is unique and is attained throughout the relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimal supports are closed under finite unions via convex combinations, producing one maximal support shared by all relative-interior optimal solutions.

children.top_down_role: Relationship between face dimension, support freedom, and active restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension–Activity Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired dimension formulas from persistent primal and dual activity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the primal-dual pair
\[
\max\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\qquad \min\{b^\top y:A^\top y\ge c\},
\]
with nonempty optimal faces \(F_P\) and \(F_D\). Let \(J\) be the support of any relative-interior point of \(F_P\), and let \(K=\{j:A_j^\top y=c_j\text{ for every }y\in F_D\}\). Then
\[
\dim F_P=|J|-\operatorname{rank}(A_J),\qquad
\dim F_D=m-\operatorname{rank}(A_K).
\]
Complementary slackness gives \(J\subseteq K\): every coordinate usable positively on the primal optimal face is persistently active on the dual optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and dual optimal-face dimensions equal ambient degrees of freedom minus ranks of their persistently active constraint systems, with primal support contained in dual activity.
assumptions_latex: Both programs attain a finite common optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim F_P=|J|-\operatorname{rank}(A_J)\), \(\dim F_D=m-\operatorname{rank}(A_K)\), and \(J\subseteq K\).

notation.meaning: dual inequalities active throughout the dual optimal face

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp equality between maximal primal support and the dual constraints active throughout the dual optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the standard-form primal-dual pair with common attained finite optimum, let \(J=\{j:\exists x\in F_P,\ x_j>0\}\) and \(K=\{j:A_j^{\mathsf T}y=c_j\text{ for every }y\in F_D\}\). Then \(J=K\). Consequently, when \(A\) has row rank \(m\), \[\dim F_P=|J|-\operatorname{rank}(A_J),\qquad \dim F_D=m-\operatorname{rank}(A_J).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coordinates usable positively on the primal optimal face are exactly the dual inequalities active throughout the dual optimal face; the same column submatrix therefore controls both face dimensions.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual programs attain a common finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J=K,\quad \dim F_P=|J|-\operatorname{rank}(A_J),\quad \dim F_D=m-\operatorname{rank}(A_J).
